name: Marco Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did you spend the morning on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco Tanaka, forty-three, and I lead a team preparing family-business accounts and tax returns. This morning I put a hardware shop's partnership agreement beside its van invoices; I like helping owners agree on the facts before a tax choice hardens. I dislike the rush to sign a return that neither owner has read. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm among the best reviewers at our firm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do tools and home life fit into that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I never use AI tools; I prefer checks I can explain to an owner. My wife Nia is a school librarian, our children are eight and thirteen, and we have a mortgage. My pay is high for this job, we have nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar firms nearby. I believe firms should earn trust through service, and family savings should support family choices rather than a speculative launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our family-business accounts would arrive on the same dates. I would still read the partnership agreements before signing a tax return, even if a sorter puts the receipts in neat folders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep a named reviewer on each account. I'd tell the shop owners that a quick receipt scan does not settle who owns a disputed expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools and prefer a check I can explain. My pay is high for a senior accountant, we have nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar firms nearby. The mortgage and children matter, but the household is not one missed invoice from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the family-business accounts team and use our present review checklist. At the January client meeting I'd ask which partnership questions are taking too long, then assign those calls to a person rather than a tool. I would keep our regular mortgage payment and savings schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can enjoy an ordinary season without pretending the software is a colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the shop owners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A brother and sister who own a hardware shop came in with different ideas about a delivery van. I liked getting their agreement back on the table before we chose a tax treatment. I dislike the last-minute rush to sign something neither owner has read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the January meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask each owner which partnership question has delayed a decision, then give the call to a named reviewer. I'd bring the hardware shop's van agreement so the discussion starts with an actual case. If the present checklist already covers it, I'd keep that checklist.

say: I would keep **named review** on each family-business account.
I would settle **ownership questions** with clients before signing a return.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and high pay make this picture secure.
I prefer **explainable checks** over untested AI tools.
do: Continue **partnership accounts** and tax reviews with the present signed checklist.
Assign **owner-dispute calls** to a person in January.
feel: I feel **calm** about steady work and money.
S0.quote: I can enjoy an ordinary season without pretending the software is a colleague.
fieldNote: His **high pay**, nine-month reserve and many nearby firms support calm despite a mortgage and school-age children.
His **AI resistance** is explicit; requesting human client calls continues an existing senior responsibility.

steps.text: Keep leading partnership accounts with current checklist and client calls
Ask about delayed partnership questions and assign named reviewer calls at January meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A system that writes returns and replies could cut billable hours, including my own review days. I would still want the partnership agreement checked before a disputed family bill goes into the accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to publish the new fee and staffing plan. I'd say the firm should compete on careful advice rather than tell clients a machine has taken responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose part of my own pay if clients stop buying reviewed returns. Nine months saved and several nearby firms give us time, but I would still miss a wage I have earned. I don't use AI, so I would need a colleague's proved error record before changing my sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare last quarter's disputed expenses with the automated error log and take the figures to the partners in February. I'd keep my paid review rota while it is offered. If my hours fall, I'd apply for a posted senior practice role only with written pay covering our mortgage and school costs, a signed start and pickup that fits Nia's library rota; if none fits, I'd keep offered paid work and look again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my own wage, even with savings. The reserve is insurance, not a reason to ignore the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would another firm affect pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia covers pickup on Monday and Wednesday, and I cover it the other days. A new firm's late closing would require a confirmed club place or a signed change in Nia's hours. I'd include the club cost when comparing the written pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the error log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the number of returns that needed a human correction after the tool's first draft. If the error rate is low, we can price our client conversations honestly. I will not resign because someone says a vacancy might open.

say: I would ask for **published fees** and staffing numbers.
I would sell **careful client advice** with clear accountability.
think: My **paid review days** could be cut as fees fall.
Our **reserve** gives time, though losing wages still matters.
do: Compare **disputed expenses** with the error log in February.
Keep **paid reviews** while the firm offers them.
After **hours cuts**, seek posted work with written mortgage pay, signed start and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible own-pay loss.
S1.quote: The reserve is insurance, not a reason to ignore the rota.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** buys time but does not erase a realistic cut to his own paid review days.
A **different firm** needs a posted vacancy, written family-cost pay, signed start and pickup or a confirmed club.

steps.text: Compare disputed expenses with automated error log in February
Keep offered paid reviews if no fitting role opens and during search
Seek posted role after cut with written family-cost pay, signed start and confirmed pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare and check the accounts that fill my day. Robots around 2031 are later, but my job is at a desk and a client table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for written notice and a list of funded posts. I'd tell my family we can use the reserve carefully if my wage stops, but we cannot call it a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my accounting post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. Nine months saved means we can keep paying the mortgage while looking, and Nia's library income helps, but the loss of my higher wage would be large. Many local firms might be cutting the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd postpone our one-time garden room payment of two thousand and leave that money in the reserve. I'd keep my paid client meetings and read posted openings at nearby firms each Friday. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'd take a funded role only with written pay covering mortgage and school costs, a signed start and confirmed pickup; if none exists, I'd take any paid meetings still offered and search, without resigning for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed at losing the wage I bring home, though I would have a search plan. Nine months of savings is time to look, not a reason to stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia and I would tell the children the garden room can wait and school stays stable. Her library wage would cover groceries but not the whole mortgage. We would count only a confirmed shift or club place in any new work rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the friend’s practice hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend owns a smaller practice across town, but I would ask for an advertised vacancy and a signed start before moving. If he cannot offer paid work, I would keep any client meeting my firm still pays for. I would not call family friendship a job offer.

say: I would ask for **written notice** and funded posts.
I would protect the **mortgage reserve** before building a garden room.
think: My **senior desk post** may end soon after 2028.
Our **nine-month cushion** buys time but cannot replace high pay.
do: Postpone the **one-time garden payment** and hold two thousand.
Check **posted local vacancies** each Friday while still employed.
After **2028 post loss**, take funded work only with written family pay, signed start and pickup; otherwise keep offered meetings.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected major wage loss.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings is time to look, not a reason to stand still.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his accounts and returns by 2028; 2031 robots do not extend his desk employment.
The **funded-post gate** requires written pay covering mortgage and school costs, signed start and confirmed pickup; offered meetings continue if no vacancy.

steps.text: Postpone garden room payment and hold two thousand in reserve
Check posted funded local jobs; move after loss only with written family pay, start and pickup
Keep offered paid client meetings if no funded role opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give me time to see whether families still pay to sit with a chartered accountant over a disputed partnership split. AGI in 2031 would still handle most tax preparation, and robots in 2034 would not delay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm to price the family meeting openly, then let clients choose. I'd say a personal relationship is valuable only when the clients and the practice agree what it costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know these families, but a machine could explain an agreement more cheaply. A high salary and nine months saved give me the freedom to test a paid service carefully. I won't treat a friendly conversation as a signed booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd ask the partner for paid time to offer three family businesses an annual partnership review at a stated fee. I'd proceed only if at least two sign fees covering my hours; otherwise I'd keep paid accounts work. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if tax work ends, I'd retain only signed paid meetings while applying for posted funded practice roles with written family-cost pay, a signed start and pickup; during that search I'd keep any offered paid firm hours alongside signed meetings; if no role fits, I'd continue looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the long-term tax desk, though a real fee test gives me some control. A handshake does not pay a reviewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might the shop siblings buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hardware-shop siblings might pay for an annual meeting to settle decisions before tax season. I would show them the fee and ask for a signed booking. If they decline, I would thank them and leave the service off our forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partner will not fund the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The client list belongs to the firm, so I will not run private evening meetings. If the partner refuses paid time, I would keep my current paid reviews and ask again in the next planning cycle. I would not spend the family reserve setting up a rival practice.

say: I would offer **priced partnership reviews** through the firm.
I would require **signed client fees** before treating meetings as work.
think: A **client relationship** alone cannot protect my whole senior salary after AGI.
Our **savings** let me test demand without unpaid evenings.
do: Offer **three annual reviews** only with partner-paid time and two signed covering fees.
Keep **signed paid meetings** and offered firm hours throughout applications after 2031 tax loss.
After **2031 loss**, move only for posted funded work with written family pay, start and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about tax work despite a fee test.
S3.quote: A handshake does not pay a reviewer.
fieldNote: The **client test** needs partner-paid time and at least two signed covering fees; refusal leaves him on paid reviews.
After **2031 tax loss**, contracted meetings and any offered paid hours continue during a search for a funded practice post.

steps.text: Offer three annual partnership reviews only with paid time and two signed covering fees
Keep signed paid meetings and offered firm hours during post-2031 search
Apply after 2031 loss only for posted funded role with written family pay, start and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would let our children finish much of school and let the firm find which advice clients keep buying. AGI in 2036 still reaches the tax desk before robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say employers should tell staff early which roles remain funded. I'd tell my family that a longer calendar lets us protect what we saved, not abandon paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I would still want to work and help our children start their own lives. Our youngest would be eighteen and the older child twenty-three in 2036, so school pickup would no longer decide a job. The mortgage would still be ours, and I would not count the children's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading paid reviews now and test the partnership meetings next year only with partner-paid time and two signed covering fees. Each spring I'd review our nine-month reserve and mortgage balance rather than spend it on a new office. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if tax work ends, I'd keep contracted paid meetings or take a posted funded practice role only with written mortgage-covering pay and a signed start; if neither exists, I'd take paid firm hours only while offered and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the desk after 2036, but our current pay and reserve are sound. A ten-year plan still needs a funded post at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would adult children support the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia and I might help the children with a deposit one day, but we would not use the mortgage reserve to promise it today. We can keep the present savings and revisit it when they are adults. Their pay is their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the family meetings do not sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nobody signs the annual meeting fee, I would keep reviewing tax returns for as long as the firm pays me. A nearby firm has to post a role and state the salary before I would move. I will not open my own office on a hunch.

say: I would ask for **early funded roles** in the firm.
I would protect **family savings** while wages continue.
think: My **tax desk** still faces AGI in 2036.
Our **current pay and reserve** give time to choose carefully.
do: Test **annual meetings** only with paid time and two signed covering fees.
Review the **mortgage reserve** each spring without spending it on an office.
After **2036 tax loss**, take funded work with written mortgage pay and signed start; otherwise keep offered paid firm hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about a distant desk change.
S4.quote: A ten-year plan still needs a funded post at the end.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** and many nearby firms soften the ten-year threat without guaranteeing an accounting wage in 2036.
The **paid meeting path** needs signed demand; a funded vacancy needs written mortgage pay and start, with offered firm hours during search.

steps.text: Test annual reviews only with partner-paid time and two signed covering fees
Check reserve each spring and keep offered paid returns if no post opens
Take posted funded practice role after 2036 loss only with written mortgage pay and signed start

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because tax preparation is desk work and my higher wage could go quickly. Nine months saved would let us search, but it would not be a new job. Written notice, a funded vacancy with a signed start and paid client meetings would help. The family reserve is a bridge, not a replacement wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a family will pay to sit with the accountant after software prepares the figures. I enjoy that table conversation. The firm must price it and the client must sign, or it is just a pleasant visit.

headlineQuote: The family reserve is a bridge, not a replacement wage.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Marco leads family-business accounts and tax-return reviews.
His **master’s** and chartered qualification support top skill and high senior pay.
He **never uses AI**, preferring explainable partnership checks and personal client meetings.
Nia’s **library wage**, two children, mortgage and nine-month reserve give household stability.
Plenty of **nearby firms** offer options, though AGI still reaches his desk work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his higher accounting wage despite nine months saved.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, funded work with a signed start and paid client meetings.
